title: Newton's laws of motion
summary: How does a force change motion? The three laws and the fundamental forces.
cards.0.p: A force is a push or a pull. It has a direction, so it is a vector. The vector sum of all the forces is called the net force. The net force decides how the object moves.
cards.0.svg#4: same scale: arrow lengths match the newtons
cards.0.key: Net force = the vector sum of all the forces acting on the object
cards.1.h: The four fundamental forces of nature
cards.1.p: Every force comes from four interactions. They are gravity, the electromagnetic interaction (all contact forces), the strong nuclear interaction, and the weak nuclear interaction. Gravity is the weakest.
cards.1.key: The strongest is the strong nuclear force, which holds the nucleus together. Gravity is the weakest, but it always attracts and its range has no limit.
cards.1.once.soru: Which interaction do contact forces like friction and the normal force come from?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The electrons in the atoms of two touching surfaces repel each other. That is why all contact forces are electromagnetic.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Gravity produces weight, and it does not need contact.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The strong nuclear force only acts inside the nucleus.
cards.2.p: If the net force is zero, an object at rest stays at rest and a moving object keeps going in a straight line at constant velocity. This is called inertia. It is why you lurch forward when a car brakes.
cards.2.svg#6: equal distance in equal time → constant velocity
cards.2.key: If the net force is zero, the velocity does not change. Being at rest is also constant velocity (v = 0).
cards.3.p: A net force accelerates an object, and a = Fnet / m. The acceleration points the same way as the net force. With the same push, an empty shopping cart speeds up more easily than a full one.
cards.3.svg#6: same force: more mass, less acceleration
cards.3.key: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A force of 1 N gives a 1 kg object an acceleration of 1 m/s². A 100 g apple weighs about 1 N.
cards.3.etk.soru: Change the net force and the mass: a = F<sub>net</sub> / m.
cards.4.p: As you just saw, if A pushes on B, then B pushes on A with an equal and opposite force. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.
cards.4.svg#4: same magnitude, opposite direction, different objects
cards.4.key: Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. They also act on different objects.
cards.5.p: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter, and it is the same everywhere. Weight (N) is the force of gravity: W = m·g. In this topic we take g = 10 m/s².
cards.5.key: Weight is W = m·g. A 50 kg person weighs 500 N on Earth and about 185 N on Mars (g ≈ 3.7).
cards.6.p: A surface pushes on an object resting on it with a force perpendicular to the surface. This is the normal force (N). On level ground with no other vertical force, N = W.
cards.6.key: N and W are not an action-reaction pair, because both act on the book.
cards.6.once.soru: A 2 kg book rests on a table. How many newtons of upward force does the table put on it? (g = 10)
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The book is not falling. The table's upward push balances the weight (2 · 10 = 20 N).
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: If the table did not push, the book would fall.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: 2 is the book's mass (kg). Its weight is m·g = 20 N.
cards.7.p: Friction acts opposite to the motion. For a sliding object, fk = μk·N, and μk depends on the kind of surfaces. With a mass of 10 kg and μk = 0.3, fk = 30 N.
cards.7.key: Friction does not depend on the contact area. It only depends on the kind of surfaces (μ) and on N.
cards.7.once.soru: Which way does friction act on a sliding box?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: Friction resists sliding, so it acts opposite to the motion.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: If it did, it would speed the box up.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Friction is parallel to the surface. The upward push is the normal force.
cards.8.p: When you push a cabinet that is at rest, static friction grows to match your push, up to a maximum of μs·N. Once your push goes above that, the cabinet slides. Usually μk < μs.
cards.8.key: For an object at rest, 0 ≤ fs ≤ μs·N. For a sliding object, fk = μk·N. That is why starting the motion is harder than keeping it going.
cards.9.p: Draw the object as a dot and add only the forces acting on it as arrows. Then write Fnet = m·a for each axis.
cards.9.key: Draw the forces acting on the object, not the forces it exerts. On an incline, N = W·cosθ, which is smaller than W.
cards.9.etk.soru: The free-body diagram of a 10 kg box at rest on an incline. Explore the arrows.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.0.acik: It rests on a 30° incline. In the diagram it is drawn as a dot, and the forces start from that dot.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.1.acik: The weight is W = m·g = 10·10 = 100 N, and it points straight down.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.2.acik: The normal force is perpendicular to the surface, and N = W·cos30° ≈ 87 N. On an incline, N is smaller than W.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.3.acik: Friction keeps the box from sliding, so it points up the slope. Its magnitude is f = W·sin30° = 50 N.
cards.9.once.soru: Which of these is not drawn on the free-body diagram of a book on a table?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The book's push on the table
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: That force acts on the table. The diagram only shows forces that act on the book.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Weight acts on the book, so it is drawn.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.yazi: The table's push on the book
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The normal force acts on the book, so it is drawn.
cards.10.p: On an incline, the parallel component of the weight, W·sinθ, pulls the object down the slope. Without friction, a = g·sinθ, and the acceleration does not depend on mass. With friction, a = g·sinθ − μk·g·cosθ.
cards.10.key: The normal force balances the perpendicular component, W·cosθ. If θ = 37° and μk = 0.5, then a = 10·0.6 − 0.5·10·0.8 = 2 m/s².
cards.10.once.soru: A truck and a marble are released on a frictionless 30° incline. Which one has the larger acceleration?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: a = g·sinθ. Mass appears in both the force and the inertia, so it cancels.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: The force pulling the truck is large, but so is its mass. So the acceleration is the same.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Being light does not increase the acceleration, because a = g·sinθ.
cards.11.p: A taut rope pulls the object tied to it along the rope with a tension force (T). Objects connected by a rope move with the same acceleration. First find the acceleration from a = Fnet / mtotal, then find T.
cards.11.key: The rope pulls on the two objects with equal and opposite T. T is an internal force, so it does not change the acceleration of the system.
cards.11.once.soru: Two boxes of 2 kg and 3 kg are tied together with a rope. They are pulled with 10 N on a frictionless floor. What is the acceleration, in m/s²?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Think of the two boxes as one object. a = 10 / (2 + 3) = 2 m/s².
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The 10 N accelerates the whole 5 kg, not just the 2 kg.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: 10 / 3 only accounts for one box. But the two boxes move together.
cards.12.p: Two objects of 3 kg and 2 kg hang from a pulley. The net force is the difference of the weights, so a = (m₁ − m₂)·g / (m₁ + m₂). The heavier object moves down.
cards.12.key: For an ideal pulley and g = 10, a = (3 − 2)·10 / 5 = 2 m/s². From the lighter object, T = m₂·(g + a) = 2·12 = 24 N.
cards.12.once.soru: 3 kg and 2 kg hang on the two sides of a pulley. What net force accelerates the system, in N? (g = 10)
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The weights are 30 N and 20 N. They pull in opposite directions, so the net force is their difference, 10 N.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: The weights pull in opposite directions on the two sides of the rope. So they do not add.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: 30 N is only the weight of the heavier object. The other object holds it back.
cards.13.p: A scale reads the normal force. When the elevator accelerates upward, N = m·(g + a). When it accelerates downward, N = m·(g − a). In free fall, N = 0.
cards.13.key: What matters is the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity. In free fall the scale reads 0, but your weight (m·g) does not change.
cards.13.once.soru: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read, in N? (g = 10)
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: The floor has to both support the person and accelerate them. So N = 60·(10 + 2) = 720 N.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: 600 N is the reading in an elevator at rest or moving at constant velocity.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: That is the reading in an elevator accelerating downward: 60·(10 − 2).
cards.14.p: Air resistance grows with speed. When it equals the weight, the net force is zero and the object falls at a constant terminal velocity. A parachute increases the cross-sectional area and lowers the terminal velocity.
cards.14.svg#3: slope is g at the start
cards.14.key: Terminal velocity gets larger with more mass and smaller with more cross-sectional area.
cards.14.once.soru: After falling for a while, a skydiver's speed stops increasing. What is the net force?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: If the velocity is constant, the acceleration is zero. So air resistance has become equal to the weight.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: If the net force equaled the weight, the skydiver would keep speeding up.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: With an upward net force, the skydiver would slow down.
cards.15.p:
• First law: if the net force is zero, the velocity does not change.
• Second law: Fnet = m·a.
• Third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on different objects.
• Weight is W = m·g.
• For friction, fs ≤ μs·N and fk = μk·N.
quiz.0.q: Masses of 4 kg and 1 kg hang on the two sides of an ideal pulley. What is the acceleration of the system, in m/s²? (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.0.e: a = (m₁ − m₂)·g / (m₁ + m₂) = (4 − 1)·10 / 5 = 6 m/s². The heavier 4 kg mass moves down.
quiz.1.q: A 10 kg box is pulled with a horizontal force of 50 N across a floor where the coefficient of kinetic friction is μk = 0.2. If g = 10 m/s², what is the box's acceleration, in m/s²?
quiz.1.e: N = m·g = 100 N and f<sub>k</sub> = 0.2·100 = 20 N. The net force is 50 − 20 = 30 N, and the acceleration is 30 / 10 = 3 m/s².
quiz.2.q: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator. Put the scale readings in order from smallest to largest. (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.2.ogeler.0: The elevator is in free fall
quiz.2.ogeler.1: The elevator accelerates downward at 2 m/s²
quiz.2.ogeler.2: The elevator moves at constant velocity
quiz.2.ogeler.3: The elevator accelerates upward at 2 m/s²
quiz.2.e: A scale reads the normal force. In free fall N = 0, and accelerating downward N = 60·(10 − 2) = 480 N. At constant velocity it is 600 N, and accelerating upward it is 60·(10 + 2) = 720 N.
quiz.3.q: When a horse pulls a cart, the cart pulls back on the horse with the same magnitude. Why don't these two forces cancel?
quiz.3.o.1: The horse's force is slightly larger
quiz.3.o.3: The cart is light, so there is no reaction
quiz.3.e: Action and reaction forces act on different objects. What moves the horse forward is the friction force the ground puts on its hooves.
quiz.3.y.1: Action and reaction forces are always exactly equal in magnitude. There is no difference between them.
quiz.3.y.2: Action and reaction appear at the same moment. There is no delay between them.
quiz.3.y.3: However small the mass is, the reaction force is always there and equals the action.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Pull the cloth, push the box, and push off on a skateboard.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The net force is the sum of all the forces acting on an object. The person on the left pushes to the right with 30 N. Set the force of the person on the right and make the net force zero.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: 30 N acts to the right and 30 N to the left, so the net force is 0. The forces are there, but the box's velocity does not change. The first law explains why.
A:adimlar.1.metin: You are going to pull the tablecloth away in one quick move.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: What happens to the plates when you pull the cloth quickly?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: They slide along with the cloth
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The cloth can only pull the plates through friction. When you pull very fast, that force lasts a very short time.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: They stay in place on the table
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Plates at rest stay at rest. Friction acts for such a short time that their velocity hardly changes. This is called inertia.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: No upward force acts on the plates.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Acceleration tells you how much the velocity changes each second. Push the 10 kg cart so that its acceleration is 2 m/s², then press play.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: a = 20 N / 10 kg = 2 m/s². The velocity grows 2 m/s each second, and the cart travels ½ · 2 · 2² = 4 m in 2 s.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The force now stays at 20 N. Change the cart's mass and press play with at least two different masses.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: With the same force, what happens to the acceleration when the mass doubles?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A heavy cart is harder to speed up. Compare the accelerations for 10 kg and 20 kg.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Since a = F / m, changing m changes a.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: With 20 N, the acceleration is 2 m/s² at 10 kg and 1 m/s² at 20 kg. Since a = F / m, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
A:adimlar.4.metin: You are standing on a skateboard and your mass is 60 kg. You are going to push your 30 kg brother with a force of 60 N.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: Who rolls away when you push?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Both of you, in opposite directions
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Your brother pushes you back with the same magnitude (60 N) in the opposite direction. The forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel. Your brother has half your mass, so he moves away twice as fast (a = F / m).
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Your brother also puts a force of the same magnitude on you. So you roll backward too.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The force you put on your brother makes him move too.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Take the 60 kg astronaut to the Moon. This scene uses real values: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth and g ≈ 1.62 m/s² on the Moon.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: The mass is still 60 kg, but the weight dropped from 60 × 9.8 ≈ 588 N to 60 × 1.62 ≈ 97 N.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A box sits on the floor. μs = 0.5, μk = 0.3, and g = 10 m/s². Change the push and the mass. The force arrows, velocity, and acceleration update right away. Find the answers below yourself.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Find the smallest push that makes the 20 kg box slide.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: The limit of static friction is μs·N = 0.5 × 200 = 100 N. When the push went above that, the box slid. Now kinetic friction acts, and μk·N = 0.3 × 200 = 60 N.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: While the box is sliding, lower the push to 60 N. Watch its velocity.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The push equals kinetic friction. The net force is zero, so the box moves at constant velocity (first law). Starting the motion took more than 100 N, but 60 N is enough to keep it going.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Set the mass to 40 kg and find the smallest push that makes the box slide again.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: When the mass doubled, N became 400 N and the limit also doubled to μs·N = 200 N. Friction is proportional to the normal force.
A:kapanis.0: First law: if the net force is zero, the velocity does not change. Being at rest is also constant velocity (v = 0).
A:kapanis.1: Second law: Fnet = m·a. With the same force, doubling the mass cuts the acceleration in half. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
A:kapanis.2: Third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on different objects. That is why they do not cancel.
A:kapanis.3: Weight is W = m·g (N). Mass (kg) is the same everywhere.
A:kapanis.4: For an object at rest, friction balances the push up to μs·N. For a sliding object, fk = μk·N.
